title: Remove.bg is shutting down: what it means for your pipeline
summary: Remove.bg shuts down December 1, 2026 at 9am CET. Unused credits expire and API keys stop working. Here's every place to check first.
body_markdown:
Remove.bg shuts down its standalone website and self-serve API on **December 1, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. CET** . Background removal moves into Canva, and API access moves to Leonardo.ai, which Canva also owns. From that moment, the self-serve API stops accepting requests, so every remove.bg API key stops working and unused pay-as-you-go credits expire.


On one login, that's a five-minute problem. Across a business, it's an inventory problem first and a purchasing decision second. A developer wired the API into the product pipeline. Someone in marketing connected it through Zapier. A storefront app calls it behind the scenes. Two colleagues have personal logins with credits on them.


So the question isn't which background remover is best. It's how many places yours is running right now. This guide covers where to look, what breaks on the day, what to save from your accounts, and how to test a replacement before the deadline.


*This guide is for teams running an image pipeline or a shared image workflow. If you're a solo seller moving one account, read*[our seller switching guide](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/photoroom-or-removebg) *instead.*


## Where remove.bg runs, and what happens to each on December 1


Remove.bg was never just an API. It shipped a Photoshop plugin, desktop and Android apps, design plugins, and apps on automation platforms like Zapier and Make. Remove.bg says its Photoshop plugin and its "other integrations and plugins" are discontinued on December 1. Any of these can live in your business without showing up in a code repository.


**Where it runs**


**What happens on December 1**


**What to do**


Your application code


Requests are refused. Seen only if the call is monitored


Engineering: search code and config; move to a new endpoint


Scheduled batch or cron job


Fails on its next run, which may be weeks later


Engineering or data: list every job's schedule; test before the next run


Code that retries failed calls


Retries against a closed API until it gives up


Engineering: check what happens after the last retry; add an alert


Zapier: "Remove Image Background" action


The step errors. After 95% errored runs (over 20 runs in 7 days), Zapier turns the Zap off


Operations: find every Zap using remove.bg; name an owner for each


Zapier: "API Request" action


With "Stop on error" left on its default ("No"), **runs are marked successful whatever the API returns** , and later steps carry on


Operations: set "Stop on error" to "Yes" now, then replace the step


Make scenario


Integration discontinued; what follows depends on the scenario's error handling


Operations: find every scenario; check its error route


Shopify or Lightspeed app


Depends on the app. Products can publish without a processed image


Ecommerce: ask the app vendor what they're doing


Photoshop, Figma, Sketch, Adobe CC


Discontinued


Design: inventory installs; agree a new tool with the team


Desktop or Android app


Stops working


Individuals: ask the teams that touch product images


Staff-owned account


Account closes, credits expire, keys stop working


The account owner: find it in expense reports and card statements


The dangerous rows are the ones nobody notices. A refused request in monitored code is the best case, because someone sees it. A Zapier API Request step marked successful, or a job that runs once a quarter, can push an unprocessed image into your catalog with no warning.


## How to find every remove.bg dependency


1.


**Search code and config for**` **X-Api-Key**` **and**` **api.remove.bg**` **.** Go beyond the main product repo: infrastructure config, scripts, serverless functions and environment variables.


2.


**Count keys, not accounts.** One remove.bg account can hold up to 10 API keys, so a single account can stand for several teams or workflows. Map each key to its owner and what it does.


3.


**Check finance records.** Look for remove.bg on invoices, card statements and expense reports. It's common to find more than one login, including personal sign-ups paid on company or team cards.


4.


**Check automation, creative and commerce tools.** Look in Zapier, Make, Photoshop, Figma, Sketch, Adobe Creative Cloud, Shopify and Lightspeed.


5.


**Ask the teams that touch product images.** That means merchandising, creative, photography, content operations and agencies. Don't stop at "do you use remove.bg?" Ask whether they have an account, an API key, a plugin, an automation or a subscription.


## What happens to your credits, subscriptions and account data


From remove.bg's FAQ:


**What you have**


**What happens**


Unused pay-as-you-go credits


**Expire on December 1, 2026.** remove.bg recommends using them before then


Annual subscription


Works until December 1, then ends. Unused time gets a pro-rata refund to the original payment method, automatically


Monthly subscription


Works until December 1, then ends. Any renewal on or after November 1 is free


Invoices and credit usage report


Download them from your Account page before December 1. **You can't download them afterward**


Enterprise API contract


Not affected. Contracts continue as normal


For every login you found:


-


Record the plan type and the credit balance. Spend pay-as-you-go credits you can use before December 1.


-


Download invoices and the credit usage report.


-


Export any processed images you still need.


-


List which API keys exist and which systems use them.


## Three tests a replacement must pass


A replacement can produce a great cutout on one image and still be a poor production dependency. Test it on these three things before it goes live.


### 1. Edge quality on your hardest products


Average catalog images won't tell you much. Test the categories that have always caused trouble: reflective packaging, fine mesh, transparent bottles, dark products on dark backgrounds, hair and fine detail, and low-resolution supplier images.


Score each category separately. A 98% overall pass rate isn't reassuring if the 2% that fail are all in your highest-value category. Set a pass threshold per category, run the same images through remove.bg and the replacement while you still can, and decide which categories still need manual review.


### 2. A price that still works at your real volume


Price your actual volume, not an average month. Include peak months, the largest batch you run, retries and reprocessing, and every pipeline that calls the API.


What remove.bg charges today, per image, on monthly billing:


**Monthly volume**


**Plan**


**Cost per image**


1,200 images


$189 a month


$0.158


10,000 images


$989 a month


$0.099


75,000 images


$5,450 a month


$0.073


Yearly billing is about 10% lower ($0.065 an image at 75,000). Pay-as-you-go costs more: from $1.00 an image for 3 credits down to $0.21 for 8,000 credits ($1,699).


*How we got these figures: read from* *remove.bg's pricing page* *on October 29, 2026. Cost per image is the plan price divided by its credits, at one credit per image.*


A pipeline that processes 50,000 images in a seasonal refresh and 5,000 the next month needs a different plan from one that runs 50,000 every month. Model a full year, then model your peak month on its own.


Weighing Leonardo.ai against Photoroom at your volume? See the full cost comparison in[Leonardo.Ai vs Photoroom](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/remove-bg-api-cost-leonardo-ai-vs-photoroom) .


### 3. A change small enough to ship before the deadline


The replacement has to fit how you operate: keys and permissions, usage reporting by team, monitoring and logging, and support. Ask three questions:


-


Can you tell which request failed, which application sent it, and whether it hit ten images or ten thousand?


-


Can you split usage and cost by team?


-


Can you rotate keys without taking the pipeline down?


Then test the move itself. Run the replacement next to remove.bg on a small slice of production traffic. Compare outputs and failure rates, and check that downstream systems behave before you switch everything over. Keep the change small enough to roll back before December 1.


## What to do this week, by mid-November, and before December 1


**Phase**


**What to do**


**Done when**


Find: now to November 16


Inventory every dependency in the table above. Record owner, account and key for each. Download invoices and usage reports. Set "Stop on error" to "Yes" on Zapier API Request steps


Every known dependency is listed and account records are saved


Test: by November 23


Run the three tests on real production images and workflows, including any unusual parameters. Test rollback


Every test passes and rollback works


Switch: by November 27


Move traffic in stages, monitor, then remove the last remove.bg calls


Every workflow runs without remove.bg, with a few days to spare


Three tips:


-


**Start finding now.** Monthly and quarterly jobs only show up when they run. If time gets tight, shorten testing, not finding.


-


**Sort calls into standard and unusual.** Standard calls can move quickly. Anything using less common parameters needs its own test.


-


**Leave buffer.** Aim to finish by November 27, so a failed switch still has a day or two to roll back before 9:00 a.m. CET on December 1.


## Moving to Photoroom


For the full tool shortlist, see our[remove.bg alternatives](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/remove-bg-alternatives) and[best background removers for e‑commerce](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/best-online-background-removers-for-e-commerce-in-2026) .


**Where Photoroom fits.** Photoroom's Remove Background API takes the same argument names as remove.bg and returns the same response format.` image_file` ,` crop` ,` bg_color` ,` format` and` size` carry over. A standard call moves by changing two things: the endpoint (` api.remove.bg/v1.0/removebg` becomes` sdk.photoroom.com/v1/segment` ) and the API key. The code is on our[developer migration page](https://www.photoroom.com/api/photoroom-vs-removebg) .


**Before you switch, check two things:**


-


**Less common parameters.** The standard background-removal call moves as is. Test anything else on your own images first.


-


**A remove.bg Enterprise API contract.** remove.bg says those continue as normal, so you can plan the move on your own timeline.


**If you need more than cutouts.** Photoroom's Image Editing API (Plus plan) adds AI Relighting, AI Expand, AI Ironing, Ghost Mannequin and Flat Lay to the same pipeline, at $0.10 an image whatever edits a call combines.


**Testing on your own images.** New API accounts get 10 free production calls without a watermark. A sandbox key adds watermarked test calls for checking output. Both are for testing, not for production volume.


To weigh the two products in detail, see[Photoroom vs remove.bg](https://www.photoroom.com/comparisons/photoroom-vs-remove-bg) .


## Migrate the pipeline, not just the endpoint


Treat December 1 as a forced pipeline audit. Find every place remove.bg is called, name an owner for each, know what happens when it stops, save your account records, and test the replacement on your real workload before you switch.
